title: Teaching as seva
tomorrow: smoke over the hills, and harjit's trucks are loading water. where to?

cards: Fractions. Kiran's little brother, Dev, is in sixth grade, their mom is still recovering, and he's been hiding his math tests in the bottom of his backpack.
Kiran asks Simran, who's good at math and bad at saying no, if she could help. Simran says yes before she thinks. Then she remembers finals.
Then she notices something at her own kitchen table: Bebe teaching Maya Gurmukhi letters on Thursdays, for free, with a pencil and a lot of patience.

teach.h: IS TEACHING SERVICE, OR A FAVOR?
teach.b: So, the question: is teaching a kind of service, or just a favor? Gurbani answers in a line from Guru Nanak in Raag Asa. In paraphrase: when learning is reflected on, it makes you a benefactor of others.
Vidya, learning, isn't only for you. Think it through and it turns outward, into help.

That's why tutoring, mentoring and teaching Punjabi or Gurmukhi to a kid at the gurdwara all count as seva, and why seva asks nothing back. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.

In the Torah, in the passage Jews say in the Shema, Deuteronomy says: thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children. There, teaching is part of loving God, spoken at home, on the road, lying down and rising up.
What's shared: knowledge is meant to be passed on, at kitchen tables, by people who aren't paid to do it. And one honest difference.
Deuteronomy's teaching is the commandments, handed from parent to child, a covenant kept in a family.
Guru Nanak's line is about learning itself, reflected on, becoming help for anyone at all.
The thing to tell a friend tonight: in both, a kitchen table is a classroom.
On Wednesday, Simran sits with Dev. They draw pizzas and cut them into eighths. He gets one right, then three.

how: Some gurdwaras run Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes taught by volunteers, and Sikhs tutor and mentor younger people as seva, without charge.

games.q: a younger cousin keeps asking how you read Gurmukhi so fast. you're busy, and she's slow. what fits today's line?
o: teach her a few letters; learning reflected on becomes help.
point her to an app; teaching her isn't really your job.
teach her only once she can keep up with your pace.
games.why: learning reflected on turns outward into help. a few letters at your own kitchen table is teaching as seva, given freely.

practice: If there's paper near you, write down one thing you know well enough to teach: a recipe, a chord, a word in another language, how to change a tire. Under it, write the name of one person who might want to learn it.
Then set the pen down and rest for the sit.
